original_value: With the recently explosive growth of deep learning, automatic modulation recognition has undergone rapid development. Most of the newly proposed methods are dependent on large numbers of labeled samples. We are committed to using fewer labeled samples to perform automatic modulation recognition in the cognitive radio domain. Here, a semi-supervised learning method based on adversarial training is proposed which is called signal classifier generative adversarial network. Most of the prior methods based on this technology involve computer vision applications. However, we improve the existing network structure of a generative adversarial network by adding the encoder network and a signal spatial transform module, allowing our framework to address radio signal processing tasks more efficiently. These two technical improvements effectively avoid nonconvergence and mode collapse problems caused by the complexity of the radio signals. The results of simulations show that compared with well-known deep learning methods, our method improves the classification accuracy on a synthetic radio frequency dataset by 0.1% to 12%. In addition, we verify the advantages of our method in a semi-supervised scenario and obtain a significant increase in accuracy compared with traditional semi-supervised learning methods.

result.paraphrase: Driven by the rapid rise of deep learning, automatic modulation recognition has advanced quickly. Many recent approaches rely on large quantities of labeled data, whereas we aim to achieve automatic modulation recognition in the cognitive radio domain using fewer labeled samples. To this end, we propose a semi-supervised adversarial training method called the signal classifier generative adversarial network. Although most earlier techniques based on this idea have focused on computer vision, we enhance the standard generative adversarial network architecture by introducing an encoder network and a signal spatial transform module, enabling the framework to handle radio signal processing tasks more efficiently. These two improvements effectively prevent the nonconvergence and mode collapse issues caused by the complexity of radio signals. Simulation results indicate that, compared with well-known deep learning methods, our approach improves classification accuracy on a synthetic radio frequency dataset by 0.1% to 12%. We also confirm its advantages in a semi-supervised setting and observe a substantial accuracy gain over traditional semi-supervised learning methods.
